key_terms.meaning: A vertical member carrying axial compression; it fails by bending sideways, not by crushing.
Any compression member of a frame or truss, usually horizontal or inclined; same buckling behaviour as a column.
Sudden sideways bending of a straight compression member when the load reaches a critical value.
Short (fails by crushing), long (fails by buckling, Euler applies), intermediate (both effects, Rankine applies).
P = π²EI/L² for a pin-ended column, where E is Young's modulus, I the least second moment of area, L the length.
Multiplier on L giving effective length: 1 (pinned-pinned), 2 (fixed-free), 0.5 (fixed-fixed), 0.7 (fixed-pinned).
Lₑ = kL, the distance between the two points of contraflexure of the buckled shape.
r = √(I/A), where I is the second moment of area and A the cross-section area; measured in mm or m.
λ = Lₑ/r, a pure number; large λ means a slender, buckling-prone member.
σ_cr = π²E/λ², the axial stress at which buckling begins.
Valid only while σ_cr ≤ proportional limit; use it only for λ above about 100 for mild steel.
a = σ_c/(π²E), where σ_c is the crushing stress; units m²/N so that aλ² is dimensionless.
P = σ_c A/(1 + aλ²); gives a safe value for short, intermediate and long columns alike.
σ_θ = pd/(2t) in a thin closed cylinder of internal diameter d, thickness t, internal pressure p.
σ_L = pd/(4t) in a closed thin cylinder; exactly half the hoop stress.
Wall thickness less than about d/20, so the stress is taken constant across the wall.
σ_r = A − B/r² and σ_θ = A + B/r² for a thick cylinder, with constants A and B found from the two surface pressures.
An outer tube shrunk onto an inner tube; the interference leaves residual stresses that share the pressure load.

takeaways: A compression member does not fail by crushing alone: once slender, it bends sideways and the load capacity drops sharply.
Every end condition uses the same Euler formula if L is replaced by the effective length kL.
The slenderness ratio Lₑ/r alone fixes the critical stress through σ_cr = π²E/λ², so geometry decides, not just material.
Euler's formula is only valid while the critical stress stays below the proportional limit; beyond that it grossly overestimates strength.
The Rankine-Gordon formula blends crushing and buckling and stays safe at every slenderness, which is why design codes favour it.
In a thin closed cylinder the hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so the wall is always governed by the hoop direction.
A thin sphere carries σ = pd/(4t) in every direction, which is half the cylinder hoop stress for the same thickness and pressure.
In a thick cylinder, hoop stress varies through the wall and is largest at the bore, so uniform-stress theory of thin shells fails.
A compound (shrunk-fit) cylinder works better than a single thick tube because pre-compression at the bore cancels part of the pressure stress.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a clean derivation with labelled sketches, correct end-condition constants, and a numerical check against the proportional limit before a formula is declared valid.

bank.q: Define a column and a strut. Explain the classification of columns as short, long and intermediate, and state how each type fails.
outline: Column carries pure axial compression and bends sideways; strut is the general term for a compression member of a frame.
Short column: fails by crushing, stress controls, Euler does not apply.
Long column: fails by buckling at Euler's load, crushing stress never reached.
Intermediate: failure by combined crushing and buckling, Rankine-Gordon used.
Brief mention of slenderness ratio as the deciding number.

bank.q: Sketch the four standard end conditions of a column and state the end-condition factor k for each. Explain what the effective length physically means.
outline: Pinned-pinned k = 1, fixed-free k = 2, fixed-fixed k = 0.5, fixed-pinned (guided) k = 0.7.
Effective length is the distance between successive points of contraflexure of the buckled shape.
Free length and effective length differ; a fixed-fixed column can carry four times the pin-ended load.
Correct sketches of the buckled axis for each case.

bank.q: Derive Euler's crippling load for a column with both ends hinged, starting from the differential equation of the elastic curve.
outline: Take a section at x, deflection y; bending moment M = −P y about the undeflected axis.
Use EI d²y/dx² = M to get d²y/dx² + (P/EI) y = 0.
Solution y = C₁ sin(αx) + C₂ cos(αx) with α² = P/EI.
Boundary conditions y = 0 at x = 0 and x = L give αL = nπ.
Smallest non-zero root gives P = π²EI/L²; state meaning of E, I, L.

bank.q: Derive the expressions for hoop stress and longitudinal stress in a thin cylindrical shell closed at both ends and carrying internal pressure p.
outline: Hoop: cut the cylinder along a diameter and take half-shell equilibrium; 2σ_θ t L = p d L.
Result σ_θ = pd/(2t).
Longitudinal: cut across the axis; σ_L (πdt) = p (πd²/4).
Result σ_L = pd/(4t), exactly half the hoop stress.
State the thin-shell assumption t ≤ d/20 and that stresses are uniform through the wall.

bank.q: A mild steel tube of length 3 m, external diameter 80 mm and internal diameter 70 mm, is used as a pin-ended column. Taking E = 200 GPa, find Euler's crippling load and the critical stress.
outline: Least second moment of area I = π(d_o⁴ − d_i⁴)/64, converted to metres.
Area A and then r = √(I/A).
Effective length Lₑ = L for pinned ends.
P = π²EI/Lₑ², answer in kN.
Critical stress σ_cr = P/A; compare with the proportional limit before accepting the result.

bank.q: A cast iron hollow column, 3 m long, external diameter 150 mm and internal diameter 100 mm, is fixed at both ends. Using the Rankine-Gordon formula with σ_c = 550 MPa and a = 1/1600, find the safe load for a factor of safety of 3.
outline: Compute I, A and r, then λ = Lₑ/r with Lₑ = 0.5L for fixed ends.
Write P_R = σ_c A/(1 + aλ²) with A in m², stress in Pa.
Carry units consistently; quote the crippling load in kN.
Divide by the factor of safety for the safe load.
Note that Rankine-Gordon is valid at this slenderness where Euler would not be.

bank.q: A thin cylindrical shell of 1.2 m internal diameter and 10 mm wall thickness carries an internal pressure of 1.5 MPa. Take E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio = 0.3. Find the hoop stress, the longitudinal stress, the change in diameter and the change in volume.
outline: σ_θ = pd/(2t) = 90 MPa; σ_L = pd/(4t) = 45 MPa.
Hoop strain ε_θ = (σ_θ − νσ_L)/E; diameter change = ε_θ d.
Longitudinal strain ε_L = (σ_L − νσ_θ)/E.
Volumetric strain ε_v = 2ε_θ + ε_L, or pd(5 − 4ν)/(4tE).
Volume change = ε_v × (πd²/4)L; check the shell is thin, t ≤ d/20.

bank.q: A thick cylinder has internal radius 60 mm and external radius 120 mm. It carries an internal pressure of 60 MPa and zero external pressure. Find Lame's constants A and B and plot the hoop and radial stress variation through the wall.
outline: Boundary conditions σ_r = −60 MPa at r = 0.06 m and σ_r = 0 at r = 0.12 m.
Solve A − B/r² for the two radii to get B and then A.
Hoop stress σ_θ = A + B/r², maximum at the bore.
Radial stress is zero at the outer surface and −p at the bore.
Sketch: σ_θ falls from a maximum at the bore, σ_r rises from −p to zero.

bank.q: An outer tube of 200 mm external diameter and 150 mm internal diameter is shrunk onto a solid inner tube of 150 mm diameter with a diametral interference of 0.1 mm. Taking E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio = 0.3, find the shrinkage pressure at the interface and the hoop stress at the bore of the outer tube.
outline: Radial interference is half the diametral value; write the radial deflection of each tube in terms of the interface pressure.
Sum of the magnitudes of the two radial deflections equals the interference.
Solve for the shrinkage pressure.
Apply Lame's equations to the outer tube with p at the inner surface and zero outside.
State that the bore of the outer tube gets a compressive residual hoop stress.

bank.q: A column has a slenderness ratio of 60 and is made of steel with E = 200 GPa and yield strength 250 MPa. Explain whether Euler's formula may be used, and compare the Euler critical stress with the Rankine-Gordon estimate.
outline: Compute σ_cr = π²E/λ² = π² × 200 000/3600 MPa.
Compare with the proportional limit, not the yield strength alone.
Show that a short slenderness gives a critical stress far above the material's usable stress.
Rankine-Gordon stays below the crushing stress at every slenderness and is therefore the safe choice.
Conclude that Euler is a theoretical upper bound for long columns only.

bank.q: Compare Euler's, Rankine-Gordon's and the secant formulas for a column carrying an eccentric load. Explain why Euler fails badly at low slenderness and why Rankine-Gordon never does.
outline: Euler assumes a perfectly straight column, purely axial load, and elastic material.
Euler's hyperbola tends to infinity as the slenderness falls, which is physically impossible.
Rankine-Gordon is a reciprocal combination of crushing and buckling loads, so it is bounded by both.
The secant formula P/A = σ_max/[1 + (ec/r²) sec(...)] brings in eccentricity e and initial curvature.
Conclusion: buckling theories are upper bounds, eccentricity reduces capacity, and design must use the safe formula.

bank.q: Explain why the hoop stress in a thick cylinder is not uniform through the wall, and show with Lame's equations how a compound cylinder gives a more even stress distribution than a single tube.
outline: In a thick wall, material near the bore carries a much larger hoop stress than material near the outside.
Lame: σ_θ = A + B/r²; the 1/r² term is what makes the distribution non-uniform.
A single thick tube must therefore be over-thick at the outside, which is inefficient.
Shrink fit puts the outer tube in tension and the inner tube in compression before pressure is applied.
Under working pressure the residual and pressure stresses partly cancel, giving a lower peak hoop stress at the bore.

bank.q: For a closed vessel of given diameter, pressure and material, compare the wall thickness needed if it is made as a thin cylinder, a thin sphere and a thick cylinder. State when the thin-shell idealisation becomes unacceptable.
outline: Cylinder hoop stress pd/(2t); sphere stress pd/(4t), so half the thickness for equal stress.
Thin-shell assumption valid only for t ≤ d/20; the error grows as t/d increases.
Thick cylinder needs Lame's theory because the hoop stress peaks at the bore at about twice the mean value.
Weight, fabrication cost and end closures decide the practical choice.
Conclude with when each idealisation is acceptable.

glossary.def: A straight member carrying an axial compressive load, usually vertical.
A compression member in a frame or truss, of any orientation.
Loss of stability of a compression member by sideways bending at a critical load.
The critical axial load at which a column just begins to buckle.
The equivalent pin-ended length kL that buckles at the same load as the real column.
The dimensionless ratio λ = Lₑ/r of effective length to radius of gyration.
r = √(I/A), a measure of how far the area is spread from the centroid.
The smallest I about any centroidal axis; buckling always occurs about that axis.
The stress up to which stress is proportional to strain; above it Hooke's law fails.
The material constant a = σ_c/(π²E) used in the Rankine-Gordon formula.
The circumferential tensile stress in a shell wall due to internal pressure.
The axial tensile stress in a closed shell due to pressure on the end plates.
A shell whose wall thickness is small compared with its diameter, about t ≤ d/20.
The fractional change in the enclosed volume of a shell under pressure.
The radial and hoop stress expressions for a thick cylinder, in terms of two constants A and B.
The direct stress acting perpendicular to the cylinder wall; equals −p at a pressure surface.
Two or more tubes shrunk one onto another so that residual stresses share the pressure load.
A joint made by making the outer tube slightly smaller than the inner tube and heating it to assemble.
The amount by which the outer member is smaller than the inner member before assembly.
A column formula for eccentric loading that includes the secant of a term containing the eccentricity.
The ratio of the failure load or stress to the working load or stress.
A shell with equal curvature in all directions; carries equal stress in every membrane direction.
